notes.body:
In the first four stages of love, every movement of the heart is ultimately a movement toward the lover's own experience. Even something as tender as غَرام — the clinging ache where a person stares at photographs and rereads old messages — is, at its core, a form of self-management. The beloved's image becomes a medicine the lover administers to themselves, a way of dulling the pain of distance.

This is what it means when we say the self (نفس) is still present in these stages. Whenever the lover asks, even silently — *what do I feel near this person, what fills me when I think of them?* — that is نفس at work. There is nothing cruel in this. It is simply not yet love directed outward toward another.

What shifts at pure love (وُد) is the direction of the gaze. The love has been refined — صَفوَۃُ الْمَحَبَّۃ, cleared of sediment — until the lover's own hungers no longer cloud it. **The question is no longer what the beloved gives, but what the lover can give.** This is why pure love does not change when beauty fades, when the beloved grows ill, when usefulness disappears. The wife who stays when her husband's face is scarred, the husband who remains though his wife can no longer serve him — these are people whose love was never built on what the beloved was producing for them.

The test is simple and pitiless: what happens to the love when the beloved can no longer give the lover anything? If it fades, it was not directed at the beloved at all — it was directed at the self, with the beloved as its instrument. That is the moment we know the نفس has finally stepped aside.

etymology: نفس (self/soul): root ن-ف-س, connected to the act of breathing. تَنَفَّسَ in the Quran means the dawn exhaled — the morning releasing its first breath. From this physical intimacy of breath comes نَفْس: the animating interior of a person, the self that belongs irreducibly to the one living it. What breathes cannot be shared; neither can the نفس.

وُد (pure love): root و-د-د. The doubling of the final letter carries persistence — something that keeps returning warmth, like an ember that cannot quite go out. وَدُود appears in the Quran as a name of Allah: the One whose love is constant and self-giving, never exhausted by the needs of those it reaches toward. مَوَدَّة is the love Allah placed between husband and wife.

صَفوَۃُ (the purest part): root ص-ف-و, meaning for water or sky to become clear — sediment settling, leaving only what is clean. صَفَاةٌ is a smooth bare rock with nothing clinging to its surface. صَفوَۃُ الشَّيء is the clearest, truest portion of a thing after everything murky has been allowed to drop away.

In the powerful image of the vine and the tree used to explain the concept of ‘عشق’ (passionate love), the roles can be understood through the effect one has on the other. The vine, which wraps itself around the tree, represents the lover (‘عاشق’), and the tree, which is enveloped and ultimately consumed, represents the beloved (‘معشوق’). This analogy beautifully and intensely captures the all-consuming nature of this elevated form of love.

The phrase that the tree "kills itself so that its beloved can love" is a poetic way of describing the **complete self-annihilation of the lover**. In this stage of love, the lover's own identity, desires, and very existence are willingly sacrificed for the sake of the beloved. It is not that the vine, as the beloved, is actively "taking" in a selfish way; rather, the lover, as the tree, gives everything, dissolving its own being into the identity of the one it loves. The tree's life force is drawn out and transferred to the vine, symbolizing how the lover's entire focus and essence are poured into the beloved until nothing of the self remains.

This is not a destructive act in a negative sense, but the ultimate expression of devotion. The lover finds their own fulfillment and purpose in this effacement, enjoying the "suffering" and constriction because it is for the beloved. The "death" of the tree, therefore, is the "life" of the love itself. It signifies that the lover's ego has been completely overcome, and their existence has merged with that of the beloved, which is the ultimate goal of ‘عشق’.

***

عشق (passionate love): from the root ع-ش-ق, connected to the noun ‘عشقة’, the name for a type of ivy. The imagery is of a vine that clings to, cleaves to, and envelops a tree so completely that it can cause the tree to wither. This illustrates how this intense form of love surrounds and pierces the heart of the lover (‘عاشق’), leading to a state of self-effacement before the beloved (‘معشوق’).

notes.body:
The two stages differ not in the fact of service but in the quality of the will behind it. At the stage of تیم, the lover has been so overtaken by love that their whole orientation shifts toward the beloved, and something in the heart cries out with genuine eagerness: **"What can I do for you?"** The joy is in the offering itself — in finding ways to be of use. The lover is still initiating, still reaching toward the beloved from heartfelt desire.

What lifts عبد higher is not a greater willingness to serve but the **complete surrender of one's own will**. The lover no longer decides how to serve, because the word of the beloved has become their only instruction. When the beloved says "jump," the lover does not weigh the request — they ask only "how high?" That unconditional obedience is what the root of عبد carries in its very bones.

This is why عبد became the most exalted title of the prophet ﷺ. On the night of the ascension, Allah did not call him prophet or messenger — he called him عبده, **His slave**. The poet asks: "You claim to love your God and yet you disobey him?" Where عبودیۃ is real, disobedience becomes inconceivable.

So the distance between these two stations is the distance between a servant who rushes forward and a self that has **quietly ceased to exist**. تیم is the lover asking how they can help; عبد is the lover who has stopped asking, because their own wanting no longer speaks.
notes.anchor: The تیم is a word used for a slave, but its not at the level of an عبد
notes.quote: The تیم is a word used for a slave, but its not at the level of an عبد
etymology: تیم (devoted slave): from the root ت-م-م (تمم), meaning to be complete, to bring something to fullness — as in تَمَام, wholeness itself. When this root flows into تیم, it points to a devotion that has reached totality: the heart is entirely given over to the beloved, holding nothing back, completed by the one it loves.

عبد (slave, worshipper): from the root ع-ب-د (عبد), holding slavery and worship as a single meaning. In the Quran, عَبَدَ is to worship, عَابِد is the one who worships, عَبْد the slave. At the root's core is a being who belongs entirely to another — will, movement, and existence all oriented toward the master.

notes.body:
### رسول and عبد — Messenger and Slave

رسول names a function — the one who carries a message. A messenger is defined by his task: deliver these words, complete this mission. The role is noble, but **it is about what you do, not who you are** to the one who sent you.

عبد tells a different story. In the ten stages of love we have been walking through, تعبد is the stage of complete, unconditional obedience — where the lover asks no questions and needs no reasons, because the pleasure of the beloved is reason enough. To be called عبد by Allah is not to be diminished; it is to be claimed. **The language of belonging, not assignment.**

Consider what Allah chose when He wished to describe the Prophet at his most exalted moment — the night of the ascension, when no human had ever been taken so close:

سُبْحَنَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًۭا
Glorious is the one who took his slave on a journey in the night.
Al-Isra 17:1

Not "His messenger." Not "His prophet." His slave — because at that moment, the relationship was not about a task to be performed. **It was about an intimacy too sacred for any other word.**

رسول implies distance: there is a sender, a message, a recipient somewhere else. عبد implies closeness — you belong entirely to the one who possesses you, and that possession, when it is Allah's, is the highest station a soul can occupy. Love at its deepest moves from doing to being, from carrying out the beloved's wishes to becoming so absorbed in the beloved that no self remains to negotiate with. The Quran's choice was not accidental: **the Prophet, in that supreme moment, was not merely Allah's instrument — he was Allah's own.**
